_note: “Did you know?” box on the printable sheet of a word set (src/pages/vocabolario/stampa/[set].astro): two or three short facts about Italian and life in Italy, tied to the words of the unit, in the English of the level. Machine draft 2026-11-15, not yet reviewed by a teacher. General orientation only, not legal advice. Units b2-37 to b2-60 have no Italian word list yet, so they carry general language tips until the units exist.
a1-01: On the phone, Italians spell names with city names: ‘A come Ancona, B come Bologna, C come Como’.
With strangers you say ‘Come si chiama?’ (formal, ‘Lei’). With friends you say ‘Come ti chiami?’.
Forms often ask for ‘Cognome’ (surname) first and ‘Nome’ (first name) second.
a1-02: ‘I nonni’ means grandparents. ‘I fratelli’ can mean brothers, or brothers and sisters together.
With singular family words there is no article after ‘my’: ‘mia madre’, ‘mio fratello’. In the plural it comes back: ‘i miei fratelli’.
‘Genitori’ means parents. ‘Parenti’ means relatives in general.
a1-03: Adjectives for feelings agree with the speaker: a man says ‘Sono contento’, a woman says ‘Sono contenta’.
‘Sensibile’ means sensitive, not sensible. The word for sensible is ‘sensato’.
‘Mi dispiace’ (I'm sorry) is literally ‘it displeases me’.
a1-04: ‘Piano terra’ is the ground floor. ‘Primo piano’ is the floor above it, like the British first floor.
Flats are often described by number of rooms: ‘bilocale’ is two rooms, ‘trilocale’ is three.
‘Camera’ is a room, often a bedroom: ‘camera da letto’. ‘Stanza’ also means room.
a1-05: ‘Il mobile’ is one piece of furniture, ‘i mobili’ is the furniture.
Masculine nouns that start with s + consonant take ‘lo’ and ‘gli’: ‘lo specchio’, ‘gli specchi’.
Before a vowel, ‘il’ and ‘la’ become ‘l'’: ‘l'armadio’ (wardrobe), but ‘la poltrona’ (armchair) keeps ‘la’.
a1-06: In a bar many Italians drink a quick ‘caffè’ (espresso) standing ‘al banco’, at the counter. It often costs less than sitting at a table.
Many Italians drink cappuccino only in the morning and not after a meal.
‘Una pasta’ can be a pastry. The plural ‘le paste’ means pastries, and ‘la pasta’ is the food.
a1-07: Italian writes the decimal with a comma: ‘3,50 €’ is ‘tre euro e cinquanta’.
‘Lo scontrino’ is the receipt. Shops are generally required to give you one.
‘Quanto costa?’ is for one thing, ‘Quanto costano?’ for several.
a1-08: Colour adjectives agree with the noun: ‘una maglia rossa’, ‘due maglie rosse’. But ‘blu’ and ‘rosa’ do not change.
‘Azzurro’ is sky blue. The Italian national football teams are called ‘gli Azzurri’.
Shoe sizes in Italy use European numbers: ‘Porto il quarantadue’.
a1-09: To say something hurts, Italian says ‘Mi fa male la testa’, literally ‘the head makes me hurt’.
Some nouns change gender in the plural: ‘il braccio, le braccia’ and ‘il dito, le dita’.
For hunger and thirst Italian uses ‘avere’: ‘Ho fame’, ‘Ho sete’.
a1-10: ‘Il medico di base’ is the family doctor. Many residents registered with the national health service choose one.
‘La tessera sanitaria’ is the health card. It also shows your ‘codice fiscale’.
‘Il pronto soccorso’ is the emergency department. The European emergency number 112 works in Italy.
a1-11: Daily routine uses reflexive verbs: ‘mi alzo’ (I get up), ‘mi lavo’ (I wash), ‘mi vesto’ (I get dressed).
Italian says ‘fare colazione’, ‘pranzare’, ‘cenare’. Many people have lunch around 13:00 and dinner around 20:00 or later.
In official texts times use 24 hours (‘le diciotto’), in speech ‘le sei di sera’.
a1-12: After ‘essere’ a job usually has no article: ‘Sono insegnante’, ‘Sono cuoco’.
Many jobs have a masculine and a feminine form: ‘il cameriere, la cameriera’, ‘il dottore, la dottoressa’.
‘Che lavoro fa?’ asks what job someone does, in the formal ‘Lei’ form.
a1-13: School stages are ‘scuola primaria’, ‘scuola media’ and then ‘scuola superiore’, for example a ‘liceo’.
School marks in Italy go from 1 to 10, and 6 is the pass mark.
‘Imparare’ is to learn, ‘insegnare’ is to teach.
a1-14: Italian uses ‘giocare’ for sports and games, and ‘suonare’ for instruments: ‘giocare a calcio’, ‘suonare la chitarra’.
Football is very popular. The top league is called ‘Serie A’.
‘La passeggiata’ is a relaxed walk, often in the evening, just to be out with other people.
a1-15: Many Italian towns have a central ‘piazza’, often with a church and the ‘comune’ (town hall).
In many city centres a ‘ZTL’ (zona a traffico limitato) keeps out normal cars, and cameras check the plates.
A pharmacy shows a green cross: ‘la farmacia’.
a1-16: ‘Sempre dritto’ means straight on. Then ‘a destra’ is right and ‘a sinistra’ is left.
On many buses and regional trains a paper ticket must be stamped (‘convalidare’) before you travel.
‘Il binario’ is the platform: ‘Il treno parte dal binario tre’.
a1-17: ‘Ferragosto’ is on 15 August, a public holiday. Many Italians are on holiday then and some small shops close.
‘Buono’ shortens before a masculine noun: ‘buon viaggio’, but ‘buona giornata’.
‘Andare in vacanza’ means to go on holiday.
a1-18: For dates Italian uses ‘il primo’ for the 1st, then plain numbers: ‘il due maggio’.
Before ‘uno’ and ‘otto’, ‘venti’, ‘trenta’ and so on lose their last vowel: ‘ventuno’, ‘ventotto’.
‘Un milione’ is a noun: ‘un milione di euro’ needs ‘di’.
a1-19: Weather often uses ‘fare’: ‘Fa caldo’, ‘Fa freddo’. Rain and snow are single verbs: ‘Piove’, ‘Nevica’.
Two seasons are feminine words and two are masculine: ‘la primavera’, ‘l'estate’ (feminine), but ‘l'autunno’, ‘l'inverno’ (masculine).
‘Il tempo’ means both weather and time.
a1-20: Many nouns ending in -co or -go add an h in the plural: ‘il lago, i laghi’, ‘il bosco, i boschi’.
Italy has the Alps in the north and the Apennines along the length of the country.
‘Il gatto, la gatta’: many animals have a masculine and a feminine form.
a1-21: Italian often drops the subject pronoun: ‘Parlo italiano’, not ‘Io parlo italiano’, unless you want to stress it.
‘Essere’ and ‘avere’ are irregular: ‘sono, sei, è’ and ‘ho, hai, ha’.
‘Andare’ is irregular: ‘vado, vai, va, andiamo, andate, vanno’.
a1-22: The past ‘passato prossimo’ uses ‘avere’ or ‘essere’: ‘ho mangiato’, but ‘sono andato’ (or ‘andata’).
‘Mi piace il caffè’, but ‘Mi piacciono i libri’. The thing you like is the subject of the verb.
‘Fare’ is very flexible: ‘fare colazione’, ‘fare la spesa’, ‘fare una passeggiata’.
a1-23: Most adjectives come after the noun: ‘una casa grande’. A few common ones often come before: ‘un bel giorno’.
‘Caro’ means dear and also expensive: ‘un hotel caro’.
‘Bello’ changes like the article: ‘un bel libro’, ‘un bello zaino’, ‘un bell'uomo’.
a1-24: Use ‘a’ with cities and ‘in’ with countries: ‘a Roma’, ‘in Italia’.
Prepositions merge with the article: ‘a + il = al’, ‘in + il = nel’, ‘di + il = del’.
‘Da’ is used for someone's place: ‘vado da Marco’, ‘vado dal dottore’.
a1-25: ‘Perché’ means both why and because: ‘Perché non vieni?’ ‘Perché sono stanco.’
Accents change meaning: ‘è’ (is) and ‘e’ (and), ‘sì’ (yes) and ‘si’ (reflexive), ‘là’ (there) and ‘la’ (the).
With ‘niente’ or ‘nessuno’ after the verb, Italian needs ‘non’ before it: ‘Non vedo niente’.
a1-26: ‘Il codice fiscale’ is a 16-character code made from your name, birth date and birthplace. It is needed for almost all official matters.
‘L'Anagrafe’ is the civil registry office of the ‘comune’, where residence is registered.
Forms ask for ‘Cognome’, ‘Nome’, ‘Data di nascita’ and ‘Luogo di nascita’.
a2-01: Ask whether the ‘spese condominiali’ (building costs) are included: ‘Sono incluse le spese?’
A rental deposit is called ‘deposito cauzionale’ or ‘cauzione’. The law limits it, so check the rules.
a2-02: ‘Il condominio’ is a building with several flats. The owners meet in the ‘assemblea condominiale’.
Many buildings have quiet hours, ‘ore di silenzio’, often after lunch and at night.
‘Vicino’ means near, and also a neighbour: ‘il vicino di casa’.
a2-03: ‘Aggiustare’ and ‘riparare’ both mean to repair. A ‘tuttofare’ is a handyman.
‘Le pulizie’ is always plural: ‘fare le pulizie’ means to do the cleaning.
‘La lavatrice’ is the washing machine, ‘la lavastoviglie’ the dishwasher.
a2-04: A traditional Italian meal has courses: ‘antipasto’, ‘primo’, ‘secondo’, ‘contorno’, ‘dolce’.
‘Al dente’ is Italian: pasta that is still a little firm when you bite it.
‘Prosciutto cotto’ is cooked ham, ‘prosciutto crudo’ is cured, raw ham.
a2-05: Many restaurants add ‘il coperto’, a cover charge per person. Tipping is not expected like in some countries.
Ask for the bill with ‘Il conto, per favore’.
‘Buon appetito!’ is said before a meal. ‘Alla romana’ means everybody pays an equal share.
a2-06: ‘Ho il raffreddore’ means I have a cold. ‘Freddo’ is cold temperature: ‘Ho freddo’.
‘Ho mal di gola’ is a sore throat, ‘Ho la febbre’ is I have a fever.
In many areas a ‘guardia medica’ service helps when your doctor is closed, at night and at weekends.
a2-07: Many pharmacies take turns to stay open at night and on Sundays: ‘farmacia di turno’.
‘La ricetta’ means both prescription and recipe.
‘Compresse’ are tablets, ‘sciroppo’ is syrup, ‘pomata’ is ointment.
a2-08: ‘Taglio e piega’ at the hairdresser (‘parrucchiere’) means cut and blow-dry.
With body parts Italian uses the article, not ‘my’: ‘Mi lavo le mani’, ‘Mi lavo i denti’.
‘Fare la doccia’ is to have a shower, ‘fare il bagno’ is to take a bath or swim.
a2-09: A CV is called ‘curriculum vitae’ or ‘CV’. The Europass format is also known.
Many Italian CVs end with a line giving consent to data processing.
A cover letter starts ‘Gentile Signora Rossi’ and often ends ‘Cordiali saluti’.
a2-10: ‘Il collega’ and ‘la collega’ have the same form, only the article changes.
In many workplaces colleagues use ‘tu’, but with a boss or clients ‘Lei’ is common.
‘Una riunione’ is a meeting. ‘Il capo’ is the boss.
a2-11: ‘Frequentare un corso’ means to attend a course, not to ‘frequent’ it.
‘Iscriversi’ means to enrol: ‘Mi sono iscritto a un corso di italiano’.
‘CPIA’ centres run courses for adults, including Italian for foreigners.
a2-12: In everyday Italian ‘il bancomat’ is both the cash machine and the debit card.
An Italian IBAN starts with ‘IT’ and has 27 characters.
‘Un bonifico’ is a bank transfer, ‘un prelievo’ is a withdrawal.
a2-13: At ‘Poste Italiane’ many people pay bills with a ‘bollettino’ and collect parcels. Offices often use number tickets.
‘Il francobollo’ is a stamp. You can often buy stamps at a ‘tabaccheria’ too.
a2-14: ‘RC auto’ is the compulsory liability insurance for cars.
‘Una pratica’ is a file or case at an office: ‘aprire una pratica’.
For some documents you need a ‘marca da bollo’, a revenue stamp that you can buy at a tobacconist.
a2-15: On the phone Italians answer ‘Pronto?’, which literally means ‘ready’.
The ‘@’ sign is called ‘chiocciola’ (snail). A dot is ‘punto’.
Formal emails close with ‘Cordiali saluti’. ‘Distinti saluti’ is more formal.
a2-16: English tech words stay unchanged in the plural: ‘i computer’, ‘i file’, ‘le password’.
‘Scaricare’ is to download, ‘caricare’ is to upload.
As of 2026 many public services online use a digital identity, ‘SPID’ or ‘CIE’.
a2-17: In Italy the legal guarantee for goods, ‘garanzia legale’, is usually two years. Keep your ‘scontrino’.
Use ‘Vorrei’ to be polite: ‘Vorrei fare un reclamo’ (I would like to make a complaint).
‘Un rimborso’ is a refund, ‘una sostituzione’ is a replacement.
a2-18: ‘Un biglietto’ is a ticket, ‘un abbonamento’ is a pass.
Fast trains are ‘Frecciarossa’ or ‘Italo’. ‘Regionale’ trains stop at many small stations.
Transport strikes, ‘scioperi’, are announced in advance, so check the company website.
a2-19: ‘La patente’ is the driving licence, ‘la targa’ the number plate, ‘la revisione’ the periodic car test.
At petrol stations ‘self’ is cheaper and ‘servito’ means an attendant fills the tank, usually at a higher price.
Motorways have tolls: you pay at the ‘casello’.
a2-20: ‘Camera matrimoniale’ is a room with a double bed, ‘doppia’ a room for two people.
‘Mezza pensione’ is half board, ‘pensione completa’ is full board.
In many towns a ‘tassa di soggiorno’ (tourist tax) is added, usually paid at the hotel.
a2-21: ‘Auguri!’ is always plural. Italians say ‘Buon compleanno!’ and ‘Buon Natale!’.
‘Pasquetta’, Easter Monday, is a public holiday and a common day for a picnic.
Public holidays as of 2026 include ‘25 aprile’ (Liberation Day) and ‘2 giugno’ (Republic Day).
a2-22: ‘Fare sport’ and ‘andare in palestra’ are the usual phrases. For team games use ‘giocare’.
Many gyms and sports clubs ask for a medical certificate, ‘certificato medico’.
‘Il tifoso’ is a fan. ‘Forza!’ is a shout of support.
a2-23: In cinemas and on TV foreign films are often dubbed, ‘doppiati’. Original language is ‘versione originale’.
‘Libreria’ is a bookshop, ‘biblioteca’ is a library.
a2-24: ‘Simpatico’ means nice, likeable, not ‘sympathetic’. The opposite is ‘antipatico’.
‘Educato’ means polite, not educated. ‘Istruito’ means educated.
‘Gentile’ means kind, and ‘Gentile Signora’ opens a formal letter.
a2-25: ‘Magari!’ is a very Italian reaction. It can mean ‘I wish!’ or ‘maybe’.
After ‘Penso che’ Italian uses the subjunctive: ‘Penso che sia giusto’.
a2-26: ‘Raccolta differenziata’ is separate waste collection. The rules and the bin colours differ from ‘comune’ to ‘comune’.
Many ‘comuni’ publish a collection calendar that says what goes out on which day.
‘Rifiuti’ is waste, ‘spazzatura’ and ‘immondizia’ are everyday words for rubbish.
a2-27: ‘Mi chiamo Anna’ is literally ‘I call myself Anna’.
Reflexive verbs use ‘essere’ in the past: ‘Mi sono alzata alle sette’.
With an infinitive the pronoun joins it: ‘alzarsi’, but ‘Devo alzarmi’ or ‘Mi devo alzare’.
a2-28: ‘Vorrei’ and ‘Potrebbe…?’ make a request polite: ‘Potrebbe aiutarmi?’
‘Scusi’ is formal and ‘scusa’ is informal. ‘Permesso?’ is what you say when you want to enter or pass.
‘Un appuntamento’ is an appointment, and also a date. ‘Fissare un appuntamento’ means to arrange one.
b1-01: ‘Tempo indeterminato’ is an open-ended contract, ‘tempo determinato’ a fixed-term one.
‘Le dimissioni’ (resignation) is always plural. Employees now generally have to send a resignation online.
‘Il TFR’ is a severance payment that builds up during the years in a job and is paid when it ends.
b1-02: The national health service is the ‘SSN’. Regions run it, so rules and waiting times differ.
‘Il ticket’ is a co-payment you may have to make for some tests and visits.
For a specialist visit the family doctor writes an ‘impegnativa’, and you book through the ‘CUP’.
b1-03: A common rental contract is called ‘4+4’: four years, renewed for four more.
‘Inquilino’ is the tenant. ‘Locatore’ is the landlord.
‘Sfratto’ is eviction. Rules for it are strict, so ask for advice.
b1-04: ‘Il permesso di soggiorno’ is the residence permit. The police headquarters, ‘la Questura’, issues it.
‘Scadenza’ means expiry date. ‘Scadere’ is to expire: ‘Il permesso scade a marzo’.
‘Il visto’ is the visa. Official sources have the current rules, so always check them.
b1-05: ‘Laurea triennale’ is a three-year degree, ‘laurea magistrale’ a two-year master's degree.
In daily life Italian graduates are called ‘dottore’ or ‘dottoressa’.
‘Tirocinio’ is an internship, often also called ‘stage’.
b1-06: In everyday talk ‘la luce’ means light and also electricity: ‘pagare la luce’.
‘Rinnovabili’ are renewable energy sources, ‘fotovoltaico’ is solar power.
‘Bolletta’ is the usual word for a utility bill.
b1-07: ‘Il mutuo’ is a mortgage, ‘il prestito’ is a loan, ‘il tasso’ is the rate.
‘La dichiarazione dei redditi’ is the tax return. Many employees use the form ‘730’.
Italy limits cash payments, ‘limite al contante’, and the amount has changed over time.
b1-08: The ‘A1’ motorway, ‘Autostrada del Sole’, runs from Milan to Naples.
‘Rotatoria’ is a roundabout. Cars already on it have priority.
‘Tangenziale’ is a ring road, ‘senso unico’ is one-way.
b1-09: ‘Il telegiornale’ or ‘TG’ is the TV news. ‘RAI’ is the public broadcaster.
‘Edicola’ is a newsstand, ‘quotidiano’ a daily newspaper.
b1-10: Fillers like ‘allora’, ‘dunque’ and ‘cioè’ are normal in speech.
‘Darsi del tu’ means to start using ‘tu’: ‘Possiamo darci del tu?’
Overlapping talk can be normal in lively Italian conversation and is not always rude.
b1-11: ‘Comune’ is a noun (municipality, town hall) and also an adjective (common).
Many towns have a ‘Pro Loco’, a local association that promotes the town and organises events and ‘sagre’.
b1-12: ‘Il notaio’ (notary) is needed to buy a property.
‘Firmare’ is to sign, ‘la firma’ is the signature.
b1-13: A ‘PEC’ (posta elettronica certificata) is certified email, used by businesses and public offices.
‘Cliccare’ is to click. ‘Il sito’ is a website.
Many English tech words stay unchanged: ‘il file’, ‘i file’.
b1-14: Many clubs ask you to have a membership card, ‘la tessera’.
‘Il tempo libero’ means free time. ‘Un passatempo’ is a pastime.
b1-15: ‘Coincidenza’ means a connection between trains, and also coincidence.
‘Il ritardo’ is a delay: ‘Il treno è in ritardo’.
‘Telepass’ is a device that lets you pay motorway tolls without stopping.
b1-16: ‘Un etto’ is 100 grams: ‘due etti di prosciutto’ is 200 grams.
In many supermarkets you weigh fruit and vegetables yourself and print a label.
‘Biologico’ means organic. ‘A chilometro zero’ means local.
b1-17: ‘Residenza’ is where you are registered, ‘domicilio’ is where you actually live. A change of residence goes through the ‘Anagrafe’.
‘Traslocare’ means to move house, ‘trasferirsi’ to move to another place.
In official texts you often see ‘cittadino non UE’ for a non-EU citizen.
b1-18: Italy is a parliamentary republic. ‘Il Presidente della Repubblica’ is the head of state and ‘il Presidente del Consiglio’ leads the government.
Parliament has two chambers: ‘la Camera dei deputati’ and ‘il Senato’.
A town is led by a ‘sindaco’ (mayor), who can be a man or a woman.
b1-19: ‘Disoccupato’ means unemployed. ‘Il centro per l'impiego’ is the job centre.
‘La partita IVA’ is the VAT number of a self-employed person.
Many employees get a ‘tredicesima’, an extra month's pay, around December.
b1-20: Many towns hold a ‘sagra’, a festival for a local food. ‘Il Palio di Siena’ is a famous horse race held twice a year in summer.
On 6 January, ‘l'Epifania’, children are told that ‘la Befana’ brings sweets.
‘Carnevale’ comes before Lent. Venice is famous for its masks.
b1-21: ‘Penso a te’ means I am thinking about you. ‘Penso di partire’ means I am planning to leave.
‘Sentirsi’ means to feel: ‘Mi sento stanco’. ‘Sentire’ means to hear.
‘Preoccuparsi’ is to worry. ‘Non ti preoccupare’ means don't worry.
b1-22: ‘Farsi male’ means to hurt yourself: ‘Mi sono fatto male alla schiena’.
‘Muoviti!’ means hurry up, in the informal form.
‘A piedi’ means on foot: ‘Vado a piedi’.
b1-23: ‘Asilo nido’ is for children under three, ‘scuola dell'infanzia’ for ages three to six.
Many families rely on grandparents, ‘i nonni’, for childcare.
For parental leave, check ‘INPS’, because the rules change.
b1-24: ‘I saldi’ are the seasonal sales, in winter and summer. The start dates are set by the regions.
Online purchases can usually be withdrawn from within 14 days, ‘diritto di recesso’.
b1-25: In an address the street comes first and the number after it: ‘Via Roma 12’.
‘Via’, ‘viale’, ‘corso’ and ‘piazza’ are different types of street and square.
At the entrance you ring the ‘citofono’, the intercom.
b1-26: ‘Il Po’ is the longest river in Italy. ‘Il Lago di Garda’ is the largest lake.
‘Etna’ in Sicily is one of the most active volcanoes in the world.
‘La Pianura Padana’ is the large plain around the Po.
b1-27: ‘Lo scirocco’ is a warm wind from the south-east, ‘la tramontana’ comes from the north.
‘Allerta meteo’ warnings use colours: green, yellow, orange and red.
b1-28: Standard Italian is based on the Tuscan of Florence. Many Italians also speak a regional dialect or language.
In ‘ce’ and ‘ci’ the ‘c’ sounds like ‘ch’ in church: ‘ciao’. In ‘che’ and ‘chi’ it sounds like ‘k’.
b1-29: Milan is one of the main cities of world fashion, with its own fashion week.
‘Fare bella figura’ means to make a good impression. Many Italians dress with care.
‘Che taglia porta?’ asks which clothing size you wear.
b1-30: Time uses ‘alle’: ‘alle otto’, but ‘all'una’ for one o'clock.
Italian calendars start the week on Monday.
Days and months are written with a small letter: ‘lunedì’, ‘gennaio’.
b1-31: The ‘volt’ is named after the Italian physicist Alessandro Volta.
‘Guglielmo Marconi’ shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1909 for wireless telegraphy.
b1-32: ‘Il posto fisso’ is a permanent job. Many Italians use the phrase for job security.
‘Ferie’ is holiday leave, ‘malattia’ is sick leave, ‘straordinari’ is overtime.
b1-33: ‘Le dimissioni’ means resignation and also discharge from hospital.
In many emergency departments colour codes show urgency: red is the most urgent, white the least.
‘Un reparto’ is a ward, ‘un ricovero’ is an admission.
b1-34: Bills for ‘luce’, ‘gas’, ‘acqua’ and the waste tax ‘TARI’ are usually in the name of the person who lives there.
‘La voltura’ is the transfer of a utility contract into a new name.
‘Intestare’ means to put in someone's name: ‘Il contratto è intestato a me’.
b1-35: ‘Domanda’ means question and also application: ‘presentare domanda’.
‘INPS’ is the national social security institute.
‘Un patronato’ helps people with benefit and pension applications.
b1-36: ‘L'esame di maturità’ is the final exam of secondary school. Its official name is ‘esame di Stato’.
‘Promosso’ means passed, ‘bocciato’ means failed and has to repeat.
‘Titolo di studio’ is your qualification. Foreign qualifications may need to be recognised.
b1-37: ‘Spesa’ means shopping (‘fare la spesa’), and ‘le spese’ means expenses.
‘Risparmiare’ is to save, also in ‘risparmiare tempo’.
‘Un conto deposito’ is a savings account.
b1-38: Italy has a points licence, ‘patente a punti’, which starts with 20 points.
‘Autovelox’ is the usual word for a speed camera.
A helmet, ‘il casco’, is compulsory on a scooter and a motorcycle.
b1-39: ‘Una bufala’ is a hoax. The word literally means a female buffalo.
‘Fake news’ is used in Italian, in English form.
b1-40: ‘Sono d'accordo’ means I agree. ‘Non sono d'accordo’ means I disagree.
‘Chiedere scusa’ is to apologise, ‘fare pace’ is to make peace.
‘Compromesso’ means compromise. It is also a preliminary contract for buying a property.
b1-41: Many ambulances in Italy are run by volunteer groups, for example the ‘Croce Rossa’ or a ‘Misericordia’.
‘Il servizio civile’ is voluntary service for young people.
b1-42: Italy has several police forces: ‘Polizia di Stato’, ‘Carabinieri’, ‘Guardia di Finanza’ and the local ‘Polizia Locale’.
‘Fare una denuncia’ means to report a crime to the police.
In an emergency you can call 112. The police number 113 also works.
b1-43: ‘Il fai da te’ is DIY, literally ‘do it yourself’. A ‘ferramenta’ is a hardware shop.
b1-44: ‘Il calcio’ means football and also kick.
The ‘Giro d'Italia’ is a famous cycling race held in spring.
‘Le Dolomiti’ are in the north-east and are a UNESCO World Heritage site.
b1-45: With ‘Lei’ the imperative is ‘Vada dritto’, ‘Giri a destra’. With a friend it is ‘Vai dritto’, ‘Gira a destra’.
‘Scusi, per andare a…?’ is a polite way to ask for directions.
‘L'incrocio’ is the crossing, ‘il semaforo’ the traffic light.
b1-46: ‘Trattoria’, ‘osteria’ and ‘ristorante’ were once different levels of formality, but today the names are used loosely.
‘Aperitivo’ is a drink with snacks in the early evening. In some cities a buffet is included.
‘Alla romana’ means everyone pays the same share of the bill.
b2-01: ‘Il dirigente’ is a manager, ‘l'amministratore delegato’ is the CEO.
b2-02: Small and medium firms, ‘PMI’, are a large part of the Italian economy.
‘Borsa Italiana’ is the stock exchange, in Milan.
b2-03: ‘Il preavviso’ is the notice period in a contract.
b2-04: ‘Il Quirinale’ is the seat of the President, ‘Palazzo Chigi’ of the Prime Minister.
Italy has 20 regions, many provinces and thousands of ‘comuni’.
‘La Prefettura’ represents the state in a province.
b2-05: Italy has one of the oldest populations in Europe. ‘Invecchiamento’ means ageing.
b2-06: ‘Il dissesto idrogeologico’ is a typical Italian phrase for landslide and flood risk.
Italy imports a large share of its energy.
b2-07: ‘Phishing’ and ‘password’ are English words used in Italian. A scam is ‘una truffa’.
‘Il Garante per la protezione dei dati personali’ is the data protection authority.
‘Autenticazione a due fattori’ means two-factor authentication.
b2-08: ‘Dato’ is singular, ‘dati’ is plural: ‘i dati sono’.
For evidence, ‘prove’ is the usual word, ‘evidenza’ is rarer.
b2-09: ‘Corriere della Sera’, ‘la Repubblica’ and ‘La Stampa’ are among the main national daily newspapers.
‘Titolo’ is a headline, ‘editoriale’ is an editorial.
b2-10: Many university exams in Italy are oral. Marks run from 18 (pass) to 30, and ‘30 e lode’ is the top.
‘Tesi di laurea’ is the thesis, ‘relatore’ is the supervisor.
The University of Bologna, founded in 1088, is often called the oldest in the Western world.
b2-11: ‘ASL’ is the local health authority. Some regions use other names such as ‘AUSL’.
‘Vaccinazione’ and ‘screening’ are words from prevention programmes.
b2-12: A ‘psichiatra’ is a medical doctor, a ‘psicologo’ is not.
‘Burnout’ and ‘stress’ are English words used in Italian.
‘Avere l'ansia’ is a common phrase for feeling anxious.
b2-13: Italian citizenship has been mainly based on descent, ‘ius sanguinis’. The rules have changed recently, so check an official source.
‘AIRE’ is the register of Italians living abroad.
b2-14: Italy has more UNESCO World Heritage sites than any other country, about 60 as of 2025.
Italians name centuries with short words: ‘il Duecento’ is the 1200s, ‘il Novecento’ is the 1900s.
‘Beni culturali’ are cultural assets, protected by the ‘Soprintendenza’.
b2-15: ‘Ciao’ comes from the Venetian phrase ‘s'ciào vostro’, which meant ‘I am your servant’.
Letters to a company often start ‘Spettabile’. Letters to a person start ‘Gentile’ or ‘Egregio’.
‘Lei’ is the formal ‘you’. It is sometimes written with a capital letter.
b2-16: ‘Prima casa’ means first home, and it can bring tax benefits.
‘Metri quadri’ or ‘mq’ is the size of a home.
b2-17: An ‘agriturismo’ is a farm that offers rooms and meals, often with its own products.
‘Terrazzamenti’ are terraced hills, as in the Cinque Terre.
‘La Pianura Padana’ is the largest plain in Italy.
b2-19: High-speed trains take about three hours from Milan to Rome.
b2-20: ‘Il ricorso’ is an appeal. ‘TAR’ is the regional administrative court.
‘Silenzio-assenso’ means that in some procedures no answer from the office counts as approval.
‘Autocertificazione’ lets you replace some certificates with your own signed declaration for public offices.
b2-21: The main law on safety at work is ‘Decreto legislativo 81/2008’.
‘Smart working’ is the English term used in Italian for remote work.
b2-22: ‘DOP’ and ‘IGP’ labels protect product names such as ‘Parmigiano Reggiano’.
‘Da consumarsi entro’ is a use-by date. ‘Da consumarsi preferibilmente entro’ is a best-before date.
b2-23: ‘Tesserato’ is a registered member of a club. ‘CONI’ is the Italian Olympic Committee.
In football leagues ‘promozione’ is promotion, ‘retrocessione’ is relegation.
b2-24: A ‘badante’ is a carer, often living in the home of an older person.
‘Legge 104’ is a law that gives paid leave to some working relatives of people with a disability.
b2-25: Pupils with disabilities usually join ordinary classes, with an ‘insegnante di sostegno’.
b2-26: ‘Contrattare’ means to haggle at a market.
‘Venire incontro’ means to meet halfway: ‘Veniamo incontro al cliente’.
b2-27: ‘Carosello’ was a famous Italian TV advertising programme from 1957 to 1977.
b2-28: ‘Il regime forfettario’ is a flat-rate tax scheme for small self-employed people, as of 2026.
‘La Camera di Commercio’ keeps the business register.
‘Aprire la partita IVA’ is the phrase for starting as self-employed.
b2-29: ‘Consenso informato’ is informed consent. It is required for medical treatment.
‘Fascicolo sanitario elettronico’ is an electronic health record.
b2-30: ‘Verbale’ means minutes of a meeting. ‘Ordine del giorno’ is the agenda.
The Italian Constitution has been in force since 1 January 1948.
In some civil disputes ‘mediazione’ is required before going to court.
b2-31: ‘Siccome’ usually opens the sentence: ‘Siccome pioveva, sono rimasto a casa’.
‘A causa di’ is used for negative causes, ‘grazie a’ for positive ones.
b2-32: ‘Credo che’ takes the subjunctive: ‘Credo che sia vero’. ‘Sono sicuro che’ takes the indicative: ‘Sono sicuro che è vero’.
‘Dubitare’ is to doubt, ‘Dubito che’ also takes the subjunctive.
b2-33: ‘Sempre più’ means more and more, ‘sempre meno’ means less and less.
‘Aumentare’ takes ‘essere’ without an object (‘I prezzi sono aumentati’) and ‘avere’ with one (‘Hanno aumentato i prezzi’).
b2-34: Numbers in Italian use a point for thousands and a comma for decimals: ‘1.250,50’.
‘Metà’ is half, ‘un terzo’ is a third, ‘il doppio’ is double.
After ‘la maggioranza’ the verb may be singular or plural.
b2-35: ‘Staccare la spina’ is to unplug, an idiom for taking a proper break.
‘Non te la prendere’ means don't take it to heart.
b2-36: ‘Le competenze’ are skills. ‘Soft skills’ is an English term used in Italian.
‘Assumere’ means to hire. ‘L'assunzione’ is a hiring.
b2-37: Italian words are usually stressed on the second-to-last syllable: ‘parlare’, ‘amico’.
A written accent marks stress on the last syllable: ‘città’, ‘università’, ‘caffè’.
b2-38: Double consonants change meaning: ‘pena’ (pain) and ‘penna’ (pen), ‘caro’ (dear) and ‘carro’ (cart).
b2-39: ‘Gli’ sounds like ‘lli’ in million: ‘figlio’. But ‘gli’ in ‘glicine’ is a hard ‘g’.
b2-40: ‘Lo’ and ‘gli’ are used before s + consonant, z, gn and ps: ‘lo zio’, ‘lo studente’, ‘gli zii’.
b2-41: ‘Parenti’ means relatives, not parents. Parents are ‘genitori’.
b2-42: ‘Fabbrica’ is a factory, not fabric. Fabric is ‘tessuto’.
‘Magazzino’ is a warehouse. A magazine is ‘una rivista’.
b2-43: ‘Ci vado’ means I go there. ‘Ne ho due’ means I have two of them.
‘Ci’ and ‘ne’ are small words that Italians use a lot in speech.
b2-44: The ‘passato remoto’ is used more in writing and in the south. In the north speech mostly uses the ‘passato prossimo’.
A story in ‘passato remoto’ often sounds like a novel: ‘Nacque a Roma nel 1900’.
b2-45: The subjunctive: ‘Spero che tu stia bene’. Many native speakers also find it hard and make mistakes in casual speech.
After ‘Penso che’ and ‘Credo che’ you use the subjunctive in careful speech.
b2-46: With two pronouns, ‘mi’ becomes ‘me’: ‘Me lo dai?’
‘Te la’ means to you it: ‘Te la spiego’.
b2-47: With the formal ‘Lei’ they stay in front: ‘Mi dica’, ‘Lo faccia’.
b2-48: ‘Sto mangiando’ means I am eating right now. Italian uses ‘stare’ + gerund for actions in progress.
‘Ero stanco’ describes a state, ‘Ho mangiato’ is a finished action.
b2-49: ‘Si mangia bene qui’ means one eats well here. With a plural noun the verb is plural: ‘Si vendono libri’.
Italian uses the impersonal ‘si’ a lot in signs and rules: ‘Si prega di…’.
b2-50: Suffixes change the meaning: ‘gatto’, ‘gattino’ (small), ‘stanzone’ (big room), ‘parolaccia’ (bad word).
‘-ino’ often sounds friendly or small: ‘un tavolino’ is a little table.
b2-51: ‘Vivo qui da due anni’ means I have lived here for two years and still do. Italian uses the present with ‘da’.
‘Abito a Roma da sempre’ means I have always lived in Rome.
b2-52: ‘Il lunedì’ with the article means every Monday. Plain ‘lunedì’ means this or that Monday.
b2-53: With ‘dovere’, ‘potere’ and ‘volere’ the helper depends on the next verb: ‘Ho dovuto lavorare’, but ‘Sono dovuto andare’.
In everyday speech many people use ‘avere’ in both cases.
b2-54: Titles lose the final vowel before a name: ‘il signor Rossi’, ‘il dottor Rossi’, ‘il professor Bianchi’.
‘Ingegnere’ and ‘avvocato’ are also used as polite titles.
b2-55: Italy has many regional words for the same thing: watermelon is ‘anguria’ or ‘cocomero’.
Standard Italian is understood everywhere, but regional words are heard a lot.
b2-56: ‘Salve’ is a neutral hello, between ‘ciao’ and ‘buongiorno’.
‘Buonasera’ is used from around the afternoon on, ‘buonanotte’ only when going to bed.
b2-57: ‘Ciao’ means both hello and goodbye. ‘Arrivederci’ is a more formal goodbye, and ‘ArrivederLa’ is the very formal form.
b2-58: ‘Buongiorno’ is used in the morning and often until early afternoon.
Greeting a shop when entering and leaving is normal in many places in Italy.
b2-59: English has many Italian words: ‘studio’, ‘graffiti’, ‘paparazzi’. The singular of ‘paparazzi’ is ‘paparazzo’.
b2-60: Dante's ‘Divina Commedia’ strongly shaped the Italian language.
